title: LLM Fundamentals: Tokens, Embeddings & Context Windows
plainExplanation: Large Language Models (LLMs) are probabilistic next-token predictors trained on vast text corpora. Text is divided into tokens (subwords). High-dimensional vector embeddings capture semantic meaning where geometrically closer vectors share conceptual similarity. The context window is the finite working memory of the model.
whyItMatters: AI Engineering isn't just calling `client.chat.completions.create()`. Understanding token budgets, semantic distance, and context constraints is critical for cost, latency, and reliability.
learningObjectives: Understand how tokenizers (BPE) split text and affect pricing and context limits
Compute semantic similarity using cosine distance on vector embeddings
Design few-shot prompts with structured JSON output constraints
commonMistakes: Assuming 1 token = 1 word (typically 100 tokens ~ 75 words in English; non-Latin scripts consume far more tokens)
Expecting the model to memorize state across independent API calls without passing conversation history

codingChallenge.title: Cosine Similarity for Semantic Embeddings
codingChallenge.instructions: Write a function `cosine_similarity(vec_a: list[float], vec_b: list[float]) -> float` that computes the cosine similarity between two non-empty vectors: dot(a, b) / (norm(a) * norm(b)). Return 0.0 if either norm is zero or vectors have different lengths. Round result to 4 decimal places.
codingChallenge.solutionHint: Calculate dot product sum(a*b), norm_a = sqrt(sum(a*a)), norm_b = sqrt(sum(b*b)). Check division by zero.

questions.prompt: If two text sentences have an embedding cosine similarity of 0.96, what does this indicate?
options: The sentences have identical character counts
The sentences share strong semantic meaning and context in the vector space
The sentences are written in different languages
The model suffered an internal calculation error
questions.correctAnswer: The sentences share strong semantic meaning and context in the vector space
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors. A value near 1.0 indicates high semantic alignment in the embedding space.

title: Building Production RAG Systems with Vector Databases
plainExplanation: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) connects an LLM to external, proprietary, or private documents. Documents are chunked, embedded into vectors, and stored in a vector database. At query time, the system retrieves the most relevant chunks via semantic search and injects them into the prompt as verified grounding context.
whyItMatters: LLMs hallucinate and their knowledge cuts off. RAG enables enterprise search, domain-specific AI assistants, and customer support bots with zero hallucination and verifiable citations.
learningObjectives: Implement chunking strategies (fixed-size, semantic, recursive character)
Store and query embeddings in vector stores with metadata filtering
Formulate grounded prompts that enforce source attribution and cite references
Evaluate retrieval quality using Hit Rate and MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank)
commonMistakes: Using overly large chunks that dilute semantic signal or exceed token budgets
Failing to instruct the LLM to admit 'I do not have enough context' when retrieved chunks lack the answer

questions.prompt: What is the primary function of chunking documents before embedding them into a vector database?
options: To encrypt sensitive data before transmission
To keep context focused and within model embedding limits so search queries match precise passages rather than vague entire books
To translate text into binary format
To speed up disk read times on the client
questions.correctAnswer: To keep context focused and within model embedding limits so search queries match precise passages rather than vague entire books
questions.explanation: Chunking isolates cohesive semantic concepts, ensuring semantic search returns precise paragraphs matching the user's question.

title: Function Calling, ReAct Agents & Guardrails
plainExplanation: An AI Agent combines an LLM with external tools (APIs, databases, web search, calculators) and a reasoning loop (like ReAct: Reason, Act, Observe). Instead of only generating text, the model emits structured function calls to take actions in the digital world.
whyItMatters: Agents turn passive chatbots into autonomous systems capable of executing multi-step workflows, writing code, booking reservations, and diagnosing complex issues.
learningObjectives: Define JSON schemas for tool calling and parse model function invocation payloads
Implement the ReAct loop: thought -> tool action -> observation -> final answer
Apply security guardrails to sanitize inputs and prevent prompt injection
commonMistakes: Allowing agents to execute destructive database commands without human-in-the-loop confirmation
Unbounded agent loops that burn infinite API tokens when tools fail

questions.prompt: In a tool-calling architecture, how does an LLM execute a function like `check_weather(city='London')`?
options: The LLM directly sends an HTTP request from its neural weights to the external API
The LLM outputs a structured JSON description specifying the function name and arguments; the application runtime executes the function and feeds results back to the LLM
The LLM compiles the Python code into machine language
External tools run automatically on the client without LLM involvement
questions.correctAnswer: The LLM outputs a structured JSON description specifying the function name and arguments; the application runtime executes the function and feeds results back to the LLM
questions.explanation: LLMs do not have direct network sockets or execution environments; they generate structured tool call requests which the host runtime executes safely.
